question: During a subtotal gastrectomy for gastric carcinoma, the surgeon ligates the left gastric artery. From which vessel does the left gastric artery arise?

answers.text: Common hepatic artery — a branch of the coeliac trunk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The common hepatic artery gives rise to the right gastric artery and gastroduodenal artery — not the left gastric.

answers.text: Coeliac trunk — arising directly as one of its three main branches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The coeliac trunk (axis) divides into three branches: left gastric artery, splenic artery, and common hepatic artery. The left gastric is the smallest but most important for the lesser curvature blood supply.

answers.text: Splenic artery — reaching the fundus via the short gastric branches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The splenic artery gives rise to the left gastroepiploic artery and short gastric arteries supplying the fundus — not the left gastric artery directly.

answers.text: Superior mesenteric artery — supplying the lower stomach via the right gastroepiploic artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the small bowel and proximal colon. The right gastroepiploic artery is a branch of the gastroduodenal artery (from the common hepatic), not the SMA.

overallFeedback.feedback: The coeliac trunk gives three branches: left gastric artery (lesser curvature), splenic artery (fundus via short gastrics), and common hepatic artery (right gastric + gastroduodenal). Memorise this trifurcation.
Correct. The coeliac trunk trifurcates: left gastric + splenic + common hepatic. This is foundational surgical anatomy for any upper GI operation.
